newsitem.title: UK: UK ad regulator notes how standards have changed.
newsitem.headline: UK ad regulator notes how standards have changed.

text.p: Britain's Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), the industry's self-regulating body, on Tuesday noted the progress it has made in its 35-year history with the publication of a booklet that shows how advertising standards have changed.

Adverts highlighted in the booklet, "Celebrating 35 years of self-regulation, include one from the 1950s for 7-Up, showing an 11-month-old baby enjoying the soft drink. The ad claimed that "7-Up is so pure, so wholesome you can even give it to babies and feel good about it."

Two separate ads for an MG Midget car and for Max Factor lipstick, both of which used phallic imagery, underscore the changes in how women have been targeted and portrayed in advertising, the ASA said. And a 1970 ad for Cossack Vodka and a 1931 ad for Player's cigarettes would not be permitted under current advertising regulations, it said.

" 'Celebrating 35 years of self-regulation' offers an insight into the impact of self-regulation on standards in print advertising and shows how the system has enabled those standards to devleop in line with public opinion over the years," the ASA said in a statement.
